title: PLC Integration for Advanced Workflows
contentStatus: Draft for DiFacto review. Title and content to be confirmed.

sections.title: Beyond Basic PLC Awareness
learningObjectives: Recall what a PLC is and how a handshake lets MoRo exchange signals with one
Understand the deeper integration competency this module builds
sections.content: Earlier integration work, such as the handshake in L3B-M4, treats the PLC as a partner you exchange signals with. This module goes further: actually programming and configuring deeper PLC integration for workflows beyond the simpler handshake pattern and the CNC tending cycle in L4B-M1. Most factory floors DiFacto works in are fundamentally PLC-controlled environments, which is why this depth matters.

keyTerms.note: An industrial computer that controls machinery and processes on a factory floor, commonly coordinating with MoRo.

sections.title: PLC Programming Concepts Relevant to MoRo Integration
learningObjectives: Understand general PLC programming concepts relevant to this integration work
Recognize the distinction between reading PLC logic and writing it
sections.content: Advanced PLC integration often requires more than just reading PLC status, which earlier integration modules covered. It means understanding or writing PLC-side logic that specifically accommodates MoRo's behavior - conditional logic blocks, timers, and state machines on the PLC side that coordinate with MoRo's own mission logic.

keyTerms.note: The sequence of steps and conditions that tells MoRo what to do during a mission.
A way of organizing logic as a set of defined states and the conditions that move it from one to the next.

sections.title: Complex Workflow Patterns
learningObjectives: Understand workflow patterns beyond simple point-to-point handoffs
Recognize when advanced PLC integration becomes necessary
sections.content: Simple handoffs, covered in earlier integration modules, suffice for straightforward cases. More complex workflows don't - think multiple machines coordinated through shared PLC logic, or conditional routing based on part type or production schedule. These require Advanced Programmers to work directly within the PLC's own logic, not just at the interface boundary.

sections.title: Debugging Combined MoRo-PLC Logic
learningObjectives: Understand the added complexity of debugging across two systems with independent logic
Apply structured diagnostic approach to this specific context
sections.content: When an issue spans both MoRo's mission logic and PLC-side logic, debugging gets harder. The first step is determining which system's logic is actually responsible for the unexpected behavior. Is MoRo behaving as programmed but the PLC's response is unexpected? Or is it the other way around? Isolate that before attempting a fix in either system.

sections.title: Version Control and Change Management
learningObjectives: Understand why version control matters for PLC logic changes
Recognize risks of uncoordinated changes to integrated logic
sections.content: PLC logic and MoRo's mission logic are interdependent in advanced workflows. That means changes to one side without coordinating with the other risk breaking the integration in ways that aren't immediately obvious. Maintaining clear records of what changed, when, and why - on both sides - is essential for troubleshooting issues that emerge after a change.

keyTerms.note: Keeping a record of every change to logic, with who changed it and why, so earlier versions can be recovered.

sections.title: Working With Facility PLC Teams
learningObjectives: Understand the collaborative aspect of advanced PLC integration work
Recognize when facility-side PLC expertise should be consulted
sections.content: Advanced PLC integration often means working alongside a facility's own PLC programming team, not working in isolation. Their knowledge of the broader facility PLC environment complements an Advanced Programmer's MoRo-specific expertise. Effective collaboration here, rather than working around facility teams, tends to produce more maintainable integrated systems.

questions.question: How does this module go beyond the basic handshake with a PLC?
options: It repeats the handshake lesson, using a different example machine and a longer worked example
It hands the PLC work to the facility team so MoRo staff never touch it
It covers programming and configuring deeper PLC integration for advanced workflows
questions.feedback: Correct. This module covers actually programming and configuring deeper PLC integration for advanced workflows.

questions.question: What might advanced PLC integration require beyond reading PLC status?
options: Understanding or writing PLC-side logic for MoRo
Replacing the facility's PLC with a controller supplied with MoRo
Fitting a second PLC beside each MoRo unit to read its status
questions.feedback: Correct. Advanced integration often requires engaging with PLC-side logic directly.

questions.question: What's the first step when debugging an issue spanning both MoRo and PLC logic?
options: Rewrite the PLC logic first, since PLC code is the likelier cause of most faults
Work out which system's logic is actually responsible for the behavior
Reset both systems to defaults and retest from the beginning
questions.feedback: Correct. Isolating which system is responsible narrows the diagnostic path significantly.

questions.question: Why does version control matter for PLC logic changes in this context?
options: It is required for the PLC to keep its warranty with the vendor over time
It lets MoRo and the PLC share a single copy of one program file
Uncoordinated changes can break the integration unexpectedly
questions.feedback: Correct. Interdependent logic requires coordinated change tracking across both systems.

questions.question: What's the recommended approach to working with a facility's own PLC team?
options: Collaborate, combining their facility knowledge with MoRo-specific expertise
Hand them the full integration and stay out of the design work
Work independently first and involve them only once the cell is live
questions.feedback: Correct. Collaboration with facility PLC teams tends to produce more maintainable integrated systems.
